newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Opposition names Lawrence replacements.
newsitem.headline: Australian Opposition names Lawrence replacements.

text.p: Australian Opposition Labor Leader Kim Beazley said on Tuesday that three shadow ministers, including immigration spokesman Duncan Kerr, would replace environment spokeswoman Carmen Lawrence pending the results of her perjury trial.
But Prime Minister John Howard meanwhile said Lawrence should be presumed innocent until and unless she was convicted on the perjury charges laid against her on Monday.

Lawrence stood down as opposition environment spokeswoman on Monday pending the outcome of the three charges, although she said she would not resign as member for Fremantle in the lower house of federal parliament.
Beazley said her environment duties would be undertaken by Kerr, while her arts responsibilities would be undertaken by industrial relations spokesman Bob McMullan.
Consumer affairs and local government spokesman Belinda Neal would represent Lawrence in her Status of Women duties.
Howard said: "Having been charged with perjury (Lawrence) like any other Australian citizen is entitled to a presumption of innocence. She should have her day in court."
The charges against Lawrence, a former Labor health minister, relate to evidence she gave in 1995 to a Western Australian inquiry.

The inquiry, known as the Marks Royal Commission, was set up to examine the circumstances surrounding the tabling of a controversial petition in the Western Australia parliament in 1992. Four days after the petition was tabled a Perth lawyer, Penny Easton, who was named in the document, committed suicide.
Royal Commissioner Kenneth Marks, who conducted the inquiry, criticised Lawrence's evidence.
She said she had not known about the petition -- criticised as an improper parliamentary tactic -- before it was tabled, but other witnesses said that she had known about it.
Assertions that Lawrence had lied to the inquiry repeatedly damaged the then Labor government in 1995.
Before the controversy, some senior Labor members saw Lawrence as a replacement for then prime minister Paul Keating.
